title: VII. An Historical Survey
paragraphs: “The medical experts have tried to convince us that the prisoner is out of his mind — in fact, a maniac. I maintain that he is in full possession of his senses, and that if he weren't, he would have behaved more cleverly. As for his being a maniac, I'll grant that much, but only on one point: his fixed idea about the three thousand roubles. Even so, I think one could find a far simpler explanation than any tendency toward insanity. For my part, I fully agree with the young doctor who maintained that the prisoner's mental faculties have always been normal, and that he has simply been irritable and exasperated. The object of the prisoner's continual, violent anger was never the sum of money itself — there was a special motive underneath it. That motive is jealousy!”

Here Ippolit Kirillovitch described at length the prisoner's fatal passion for Grushenka. He began with the moment the prisoner went to the ‘young woman's’ lodgings ‘to beat her’ — ‘I'm using his own words,’ the prosecutor explained — ‘but instead of beating her, he stayed there, at her feet. That was where the passion began. At the same time, the prisoner's father had fallen for the same young woman — a strange and fatal coincidence, since both of them lost their hearts to her at once, though both had known her before. And she inspired in both of them the same violent, characteristically Karamazov passion. We have her own confession: “I was laughing at both of them.” Yes — the sudden urge to make a joke of them came over her, and she conquered them both at once. The old man, who worshipped money, immediately set aside three thousand roubles as payment for a single visit from her — but soon after, he'd have been happy to lay his whole fortune and his name at her feet, if only she'd become his lawful wife. We have solid evidence of this. As for the prisoner, the tragedy of his fate is plain — it's right in front of us. But such was the young woman's “game.” The enchantress gave the unhappy young man no hope until the very last moment, when he knelt before her with hands already stained with his father's and rival's blood. That was the position he was in when he was arrested. “Send me to Siberia with him — I brought him to this, I am the one most to blame,” the woman herself cried, in genuine remorse, at the moment of his arrest.’

“The talented young man I've already mentioned, Mr. Rakitin, summed up this heroine in a few striking words: ‘She was disillusioned early in life, betrayed and ruined by a fiancé who seduced and abandoned her. She was left in poverty, cursed by her respectable family, and taken under the wing of a wealthy old man, whom to this day she still considers her benefactor. There may well have been a great deal of good in her young heart, but it was embittered too soon. She grew shrewd and started saving money. She became sarcastic and resentful toward society.’ After that sketch of her character, it's easy enough to understand how she might have laughed at both of them purely out of mischief, out of spite.”

“After a month of hopeless love and moral collapse, during which he betrayed his betrothed and misappropriated money entrusted to his honor, the prisoner was driven nearly to frenzy, nearly to madness, by relentless jealousy — of whom? His own father! And the worst part was that the crazy old man was luring and enticing the object of his son's affection with the very same three thousand roubles that the son regarded as his own, part of his inheritance from his mother, of which his father was cheating him. Yes, I admit — that was hard to bear. It might well drive a man mad. It wasn't the money itself, but the fact that this money was being used, with such revolting cynicism, to destroy his happiness!”
Then the prosecutor went on to describe how the idea of murdering his father had taken hold in the prisoner's mind, and backed up his theory with facts.

“At first he only talked about it in taverns — he talked about it all that month. Ah, he likes always having company around him, and he likes telling his companions everything, even his most diabolical and dangerous ideas; he likes sharing every thought with others, and for some reason expects the people he confides in to meet him with perfect sympathy, to enter into all his troubles and worries, to take his side and never oppose him in anything. If they don't, he flies into a rage and smashes up everything in the tavern.” (Then followed the anecdote about Captain Snegiryov.) “Those who heard the prisoner began at last to suspect he might mean more than idle threats, and that such a frenzy might turn talk into action.”
Here the prosecutor described the family's meeting at the monastery, the conversations with Alyosha, and the ugly scene of violence when the prisoner burst into his father's house just after dinner.

“I can't say for certain,” the prosecutor went on, “that the prisoner had fully made up his mind to murder his father before that incident. And yet the idea had occurred to him more than once, and he had dwelt on it — we have facts, witnesses, and his own words to prove it. I confess, gentlemen of the jury,” he added, “that until today I was uncertain whether to credit the prisoner with conscious premeditation. I was firmly convinced he had pictured that fatal moment beforehand — but only pictured it, entertained it as a possibility. He hadn't definitely worked out when or how he might commit the crime.”

“But I was uncertain only until today — until that fatal document was placed before the court just now. You yourselves heard that young lady's exclamation: ‘It's the plan — the program for the murder!’ That's how she described that wretched, drunken letter from the unfortunate prisoner. And in fact, from that letter, we can see that the murder was premeditated in its entirety. It was written two days beforehand, and so we now know, as a fact, that forty-eight hours before carrying out his terrible design, the prisoner swore that if he couldn't get money by the next day, he would murder his father to take the envelope with the notes from under his pillow, as soon as Ivan had left. ‘As soon as Ivan has gone away’ — you hear that? So he had thought it all through, weighing every circumstance, and he carried it out exactly as he had written it. The proof of premeditation is conclusive; the crime must have been committed for the sake of the money — that's stated plainly, written down, and signed. The prisoner doesn't deny his own signature.”

“I'll be told he was drunk when he wrote it. But that doesn't lessen the letter's value — quite the opposite: drunk, he wrote down what he had planned sober. If he hadn't planned it sober, he wouldn't have written it drunk. I'll be asked: then why did he talk about it in taverns? A man planning such a crime keeps quiet and holds it to himself. Yes — but he talked about it before he'd formed any plan, when he had only the desire, only the impulse toward it. Afterward he talked about it less. On the evening he wrote that letter, at the ‘Metropolis’ tavern, he was unusually silent, though he'd been drinking. He didn't play billiards; he sat in a corner and spoke to no one. True, he did turn a shopkeeper out of his seat, but that was done almost without thinking — he could never walk into a tavern without causing some kind of scene. It's true that once he'd made his final decision, he must have felt uneasy at having talked so much about his plan beforehand, worried that it might lead to his arrest and prosecution afterward. But there was nothing to be done — he couldn't take his words back. Still, his luck had served him before, and it would serve him again. He believed in his star, you understand! I should add, too, that he did a great deal to avoid the fatal catastrophe. ‘Tomorrow I'll try to borrow money from everyone,’ as he puts it in his own peculiar language, ‘and if they won't give it to me, there will be bloodshed.’”

Here Ippolit Kirillovitch went into a detailed account of all Mitya's efforts to borrow money. He described the visit to Samsonov, the trip to Lyagavy. “Harassed, mocked, hungry, having sold his watch to pay for the journey (though he tells us he had fifteen hundred roubles on him at the time — a likely story), tormented by jealousy at having left the object of his affections back in town, suspecting she'd go to Fyodor Pavlovitch while he was away, he finally returned to town, only to discover, to his joy, that she hadn't gone near his father. He even walked her home to her protector himself. (Strangely enough, he doesn't seem to have been jealous of Samsonov — which is psychologically interesting.) Then he hurries back to his hiding place in the back gardens, and there learns that Smerdyakov is having a fit, that the other servant is ill — the coast is clear, and he knows the ‘signals’ — what a temptation! And still he resists it; he goes off instead to a lady who has been living in town for some time and is highly respected among us, Madame Hohlakov. That lady, who had long watched his career with pity, gave him the most sensible advice: to give up his dissipated life, his unseemly love affair, the waste of his youth and energy in tavern debauchery, and to head off to Siberia to the gold mines — ‘that would be an outlet for your restless energy, your romantic nature, your thirst for adventure.’”

After describing the outcome of that conversation, and the moment the prisoner learned that Grushenka had not, after all, stayed at Samsonov's — the sudden frenzy of the unlucky man, worn down by jealousy and nervous exhaustion, at the thought that she had deceived him and was now with his father — Ippolit Kirillovitch closed by dwelling on the fatal role of chance. “Had the maid told him her mistress was at Mokroe with her former lover, nothing would have happened. But she lost her head; all she could do was swear and protest that she knew nothing, and if the prisoner didn't kill her on the spot, it was only because he ran off in pursuit of his faithless mistress.”

“But notice — frantic as he was, he took a brass pestle with him. Why that? Why not some other weapon? Because he'd been turning his plan over and preparing himself for it for a full month, he would have snatched up whatever looked like a weapon caught his eye. He'd realized for a month that any such object would serve, so he recognized instantly, without hesitation, that this one would do the job. So it wasn't unconscious at all, wasn't involuntary, that he grabbed that fatal pestle. And then we find him in his father's garden — the coast clear, no witnesses, darkness and jealousy all around him. The suspicion that she was there, with him, with his rival, in his arms, maybe laughing at him at that very moment — it took his breath away. And it wasn't mere suspicion; the deception was open, obvious. She had to be there, in that lit room, behind the screen — and the unhappy man would have us believe that he crept up to the window, peeked in respectfully, and discreetly withdrew, for fear something terrible and improper might happen. And he tries to persuade us of that — us, who understand his character, who know his state of mind at that moment, and know that he knew the very signals that would let him walk straight into the house.” At this point Ippolit Kirillovitch broke off to give an exhaustive discussion of the suspected connection between Smerdyakov and the murder. He went into it very thoroughly, and everyone could tell that although he claimed to dismiss the suspicion, he thought the subject mattered a great deal.
